memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'Along with their fellowship offering of thanksgiving they are to present an offering with thick loaves of bread made with yeast. They are to bring one of each kind as an offering, a contribution to the LORD; it belongs to the priest who splashes the blood of the fellowship offering against the altar.'" - Lev 7:13-14 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This is a surprise. Yeast has been forbidden throughout these chapters — never on the altar, never in the grain offering. And here God commands bread made with yeast.

But read carefully. This yeasted bread was a contribution to the priest, not something burned on the altar. It fed a family; it was not offered in the fire.

The distinction holds. Nothing corruptible goes on the altar. But God gladly receives ordinary, everyday bread as part of a thanksgiving celebration.

There is a lesson in that for how we think about our lives. What goes on the altar — what stands as the basis of our acceptance before God — must be perfect, and only Christ qualifies. But the ordinary, imperfect substance of daily life is not thereby rejected. God receives it. He just does not confuse it with the altar.

Your cooking, your work, your hospitality, your imperfect service: none of it is your righteousness. All of it can be an offering of thanks.

Paul captures both truths. Christ alone is our righteousness: not having a righteousness of my own... but that which is through faith in Christ (Phil 3:9). And ordinary life is genuine worship: whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31).

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Am I clear about the difference between my righteousness in Christ and my offerings of service?
2. What ordinary part of today could I offer to God as thanksgiving?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, Christ alone is my righteousness, and yet You receive my ordinary life as thanks. Take today's small offerings gladly. Amen.
